reviews.overall: Em đã nhận ra Argentina tăng, Australia giảm và Thailand luôn đứng đầu. Tuy nhiên, bài có 146 từ, chưa đạt mức tối thiểu 150 từ. Ba số liệu của Thailand đều chép lệch bảng, trong khi Overview chưa nói rõ nước này đạt đỉnh năm 2006 rồi giảm. Câu mở bài thiếu động từ “were”; cụm “dramatically rise” cũng sai từ loại. Em cần kiểm tra từng số theo đúng nước và năm, bổ sung mốc 2006 của Argentina để làm rõ sự đổi thứ hạng với Australia, rồi viết Detail 2 thành ít nhất hai câu.
reviews.dataGrouping: Em ghép hai nước tăng ròng là Thailand và Argentina ở Detail 1, rồi dành Detail 2 cho Australia giảm; cách chia theo đối tượng này có thể dùng. Tuy nhiên, Detail 1 chưa nêu mốc 2006 của Argentina nên chưa chứng minh được nước này tăng liên tục và vượt Australia; Detail 2 chỉ có một câu, chưa đạt yêu cầu mỗi Detail ít nhất hai câu. Em có thể chia theo hai giai đoạn 2003–2006 và 2006–2009 để so sánh ba nước tại mốc giữa rõ hơn.

The given table illustrates how many cars produced in three countries: Argentina, Australia and Thailand over a six-year period, commencing from 2003.
Overall, there was a general increase in the number of cars manufactured in Argentina and Thailand, while an opposite trend was observed in Australia. Also of note is that Thailand consistently had the highest figures throughout the years.
To elaborate, in 2003, 755,852 cars were made, with a subsequent dramatically rise to 1,162,856 in 2006, marking the highest point of the entire chart, before falling to 999,863 in 2009. The figures for Argentina also went up from 235,088 to 466,089 for the same period of time.
Regarding the data that showed a downward trend, the number of cars produced in Australia started at 452,163 in 2003, after which it experienced a decline to 341,268 in 2006 before ending the period at 245,624 in 2009.

Overall, car production rose steadily in Argentina and fell steadily in Australia. Thailand produced the most cars in every year; its output reached a peak in 2006 before declining, although it remained higher in 2009 than in 2003.

In 2003, Thailand manufactured 735,852 cars, compared with 452,163 in Australia and 235,088 in Argentina. From 2006 to 2009, Thailand's output dropped to 999,963 cars but remained far above that of the other countries. Argentina's figure continued to grow, reaching 466,089 cars, while Australia's production declined further to 245,624. Thus, Australia moved from second to third place over the period, whereas Argentina rose from third to second.

reviews.suggestedRevision:
The two line charts compare the numbers of male and female prisoners in a European country from 1911 to 2001.

Overall, men outnumbered women in prison throughout the period. The male prison population fell early on but then rose substantially, especially between 1971 and 1981. In contrast, the female population dropped to a low in 1941 and then fluctuated before ending below its initial level.

In 1911, there were about 18,000 male prisoners, and this figure remained almost unchanged in 1921. It fell to roughly 10,000 in 1931 before recovering to around 19,000 by 1951. After staying close to that level through 1971, the number climbed sharply to approximately 39,000 in 1981 and reached about 46,000 in 2001.

The number of female prisoners began at roughly 3,200 in 1911 and declined steeply to about 500 in 1941. It then rose to around 1,500 by 1961, before dropping again to roughly 700 in 1971. From that point, the figure increased to about 1,900 in 2001, still below its starting level and far lower than the male figure that year.

The given line chart illustrates how much fish and four different types of meat were consumed in a European country from 1979 to 2004, measured in grams per person per week.
Overall,out of the studied meat types,only chicken consumption showed signs of increase in a European country.Notably,chicken consumption is highest at the end of the period,while fish consistently had the lowest figures throughout the years.
To elaborate,in 1979,approximately 220 grams of beef was consumed per person per week, making it the most widely consumed type of meat that year,with a subsequent fluctuation and a significant rise to around 240 grams in 1983, before gradually declining to over 100 grams in 2004.By contrast,the figures for chicken generally increased despite some fluctuations.It started at roughly 140 grams in 1979,after which it continued to rise and peaked at over 250 grams in 2002, before ending the period at 250 in 2004.
Regarding categories with lower data, 150 grams of lamb were consumed in 1979, before falling considerably to approximately 60 grams in 2004. A similar pattern was recorded in the figures for fish, which started at around 60 grams and then declined gradually to approximately 35 grams by the end of the period, marking the lowest point of the entire chart.

reviews.suggestedRevision:
The line graph illustrates changes in the weekly consumption of chicken, beef, lamb and fish in a European country between 1979 and 2004, measured in grams per person.

Overall, chicken was the only category whose consumption rose markedly, overtaking beef around 1988 to have the highest figure by the end. Beef and lamb fell considerably, whereas fish declined only slightly and remained the least consumed throughout.

To elaborate, beef consumption began at about 220 grams per person per week, the highest figure in 1979. After falling briefly, it reached a peak of around 240 grams in 1983, then declined overall, despite fluctuations, to roughly 110 grams in 2004. By contrast, chicken consumption increased from around 140 grams to approximately 250 grams over the same period, with small fluctuations and a high of about 255 grams in 2003.

Turning to the other two categories, lamb consumption fell from about 150 grams per person per week in 1979 to roughly 55 grams in 2004, although it rose slightly at several points. Fish followed a much gentler downward trend, decreasing from around 60 to 35 grams per person per week. Its final figure was the lowest shown on the chart.

The given bar chart illustrates the proportion of young people pursuing university education in four different countries over 10-year period,commencing from 2000.
Overall, there was a general increase in the proportion of young people in higher education in most of the studied nations,with Country D witnessing the most pronounced rise,while the figure for Country B remained relatively stable. Also of note is that Country D consistently had the highest figures throughout the years.
To elaborate, the share of young people studying at university in Country D started at 60% in 2000, with a subsequent slight rise to 65% in 2005 before growing sharply to 80% in the end of the period, marking the highest point on the entire chart.The figures for Country A also went up from approximately 37% to 58% for the same period of time.
Regarding categories with more stable trends,in 2000, 40% of the young people pursued higher education in Country B,after which it experienced an insignificant decline to 38% in 2005 before returning to 40% in 2010. A similar pattern was recorded in Country C, this figure increased minimally from 50% to around 52% between 2000 and 2010. However, this increase was still negligible compared with the increases recorded in Country A and Country D.

Overall,there was an increase in the proportions of students choosing the university for suitable degree courses, proximity to parental homes and quality of teaching.While an opposite trend was observed in the figures for quality of resources and sports and social activities. Regarding the factors that experienced a decline, the percentage of students selecting the university because of its quality of resources fell from 21% in 1997 to 17% in 2007. Likewise, the figures for good sports and social activities dropped considerably, from 19% to just 6%, marking the least popular reason for student’s university choices in 2007.
